Box Tree
BOX tree
noun
From the Latin buxus and the Greek pyxos, the box. In the AV it renders the Hebrew te'ashshur, a slow-growing evergreen of hard, close, pale timber, prized by the ancients for carving and inlay and named among the trees the LORD promises to plant in the desert.

Biblical Definition

The box tree appears twice in Scripture, both times in Isaiah, and both times as something God plants where it could never have grown. The first is the wilderness promise: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19). Every verb is His — I will plant, I will set — and the reason is given in the next breath: “that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it” (Isa 41:20). A desert does not sprout box trees. A grove of hardwood standing in sand is not an achievement of the sand; it is a signature. This is monergism written in horticulture: the LORD does not water a seed the wilderness supplied, He plants what was never there. Isaiah says the same of the men themselves — they are “trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified” (Isa 61:3), given beauty for ashes and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. The second occurrence gathers the same timber into worship: “the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). What sovereign grace plants in the waste, sovereign grace at last builds into the house of God. The desert grove and the sanctuary are the same wood at two stages of one work.

Webster 1828 Definition

A slow-growing evergreen of hard, close, pale wood; in Isaiah one of the trees the LORD plants in the desert.

BOX TREE, an evergreen of slow growth, bearing a hard, close-grained, pale yellow wood.

From the Latin buxus, Greek pyxos; in the AV the Hebrew te'ashshur.

Its timber was prized by the ancients for carving, inlay, and fine turning.

It is named among the trees the LORD sets in the desert (Isa 41:19).

It comes with the glory of Lebanon to beautify the sanctuary (Isa 60:13).

Key Scripture

Isa 41:19 — "I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:"

Isa 60:13 — "The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious."

Isa 61:3 — "To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified."

Rom 8:21 — "Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God."

Modern Corruption

“I will plant… I will set” — and the age insists the desert must first decide to grow something.

expand to see more

The corruption is synergism, and its popular form is decisional regeneration: the doctrine, spread through Finney’s new measures and hardened by a century of altar calls and sinner’s prayers, that the sinner’s free decision is the cause which turns God’s offered grace into an actual salvation. On that scheme the box tree plants itself and asks the LORD for water. Isaiah will not have it. The verbs are His: I will plant, I will set — and the stated purpose is that men may know “that the hand of the LORD hath done this” (Isa 41:20). Scripture is uniform: the natural man “receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God… neither can he know them” (1Co 2:14); the dead are quickened, not coaxed (Eph 2:1–5); we are born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13). A desert contributes nothing to a grove but the ground it is planted in.

The principle to recover is effectual calling, and with it the assurance it carries. If the box tree planted itself, it may uproot itself; if the LORD planted it, then “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6). This is why the same prophet who names the desert planting can promise that the identical timber will one day stand in the sanctuary (Isa 60:13): what grace begins in the waste place, grace finishes in the house of God. And note that monergism does not make the believer passive afterward — the tree, once planted, genuinely grows, genuinely bears, and is genuinely called a tree of righteousness (Isa 61:3). Free will is not abolished; it is liberated. The desert is not consulted, but the grove is real.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word names a hard-wooded evergreen — in Isaiah, a tree the LORD alone plants in the sand.

expand to see more

Box tree — Latin buxus, Greek pyxos; the Hebrew te'ashshur.

It is a slow-growing evergreen with hard, close, pale timber.

The ancients used it for carving, inlay, and the finest turned work.

The LORD sets it in the desert with the fir and the pine (Isa 41:19).

It comes with the glory of Lebanon to beautify His sanctuary (Isa 60:13).

Usage

"I will set in the desert… the box tree: every verb in the promise is God’s."

"A hardwood grove standing in sand is not the sand’s achievement but God’s signature."

"The box planted in the wilderness ends up in the sanctuary — one work, two stages."
